paragraphs.text:
Brainstem Mastermind
Expanded Initial Case Library
72 curated localization cases • 36 anatomical patterns mirrored left/right
Purpose and evidence standard

This library maximizes the number of playable cases while separating robust clinical-anatomical templates from rare or experimental templates. Each anatomical pattern is mirrored to create a left-sided and right-sided case. Mirroring changes the side of ipsilateral cranial-nerve, cerebellar, and autonomic findings and the side of contralateral long-tract findings; it does not create a new syndrome.

Evidence tiers: Strong = supported by established clinical–MRI series or classic reproducible anatomy; Moderate = defensible variant with published support but less unique; Rare = documented focal syndrome or unusual sensory pattern; Experimental = anatomically plausible game template requiring expert review before routine use. The 24-cell quadrant system itself is a game-design abstraction and should not be represented as a natural clinical taxonomy.
Library composition
Facilitator use
Each turn reveals one selected examination domain, followed by a mandatory full-coordinate wand placement.
All listed negative findings are treated as hard exclusions only within the curated template.
Cases marked Rare or Experimental should state that the lesion is small and anatomically confined.
If a case cannot be distinguished from its nearest competitor without pathology, imaging, or an artificial clue, remove it from the base deck rather than forcing certainty.
The facilitator should reveal the most discriminating clue late, not first.
Midbrain
Ventromedial
1. Right Ventromedial Midbrain: Oculomotor–peduncular hemiparesis
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops abrupt diplopia and left-sided weakness.
2. Left Ventromedial Midbrain: Oculomotor–peduncular hemiparesis
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops abrupt diplopia and right-sided weakness.
3. Right Ventromedial Midbrain: Partial CN III palsy with corticobulbar-predominant weakness
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops diplopia, dysarthria, and subtle left lower facial and hand weakness.
4. Left Ventromedial Midbrain: Partial CN III palsy with corticobulbar-predominant weakness
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops diplopia, dysarthria, and subtle right lower facial and hand weakness.
5. Right Ventromedial Midbrain: Peduncular pure motor syndrome with subtle oculomotor anchor
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops sudden left hemiparesis; careful examination reveals mild diplopia.
6. Left Ventromedial Midbrain: Peduncular pure motor syndrome with subtle oculomotor anchor
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops sudden right hemiparesis; careful examination reveals mild diplopia.
Ventrolateral
7. Right Ventrolateral Midbrain: Lateral cerebral peduncle ataxic hemiparesis
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops left weakness and disproportionate clumsiness without diplopia.
8. Left Ventrolateral Midbrain: Lateral cerebral peduncle ataxic hemiparesis
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate

9. Right Ventrolateral Midbrain: Focal nigral hemiparkinsonism
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

10. Left Ventrolateral Midbrain: Focal nigral hemiparkinsonism
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced
A patient develops abrupt right bradykinesia and rigidity with very mild weakness.
11. Right Ventrolateral Midbrain: Peduncular sensorimotor syndrome
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced

12. Left Ventrolateral Midbrain: Peduncular sensorimotor syndrome
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced
A patient develops right weakness with right body sensory loss but no ocular-motor abnormality.
Dorsomedial

Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

14. Left Dorsomedial Midbrain: Claude-type oculomotor–cerebellar syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

16. Left Dorsomedial Midbrain: MLF–vertical gaze network syndrome

18. Left Dorsomedial Midbrain: Red-nucleus-region tremor with partial III fascicular sign
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops coarse right action tremor and diplopia without weakness.
Dorsolateral

Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

20. Left Dorsolateral Midbrain: Trochlear–spinothalamic syndrome
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

21. Right Dorsolateral Midbrain: Tectal–lateral sensory syndrome
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced

22. Left Dorsolateral Midbrain: Tectal–lateral sensory syndrome
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced

23. Right Dorsolateral Midbrain: Lateral midbrain hemiataxia with sensory sparing

24. Left Dorsolateral Midbrain: Lateral midbrain hemiataxia with sensory sparing

28. Left Ventromedial Pons: Dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome

30. Left Ventromedial Pons: Pontine ataxic hemiparesis

32. Left Ventrolateral Pons: Anterolateral pontine sensorimotor syndrome

36. Left Ventrolateral Pons: Lateral pontine motor-sensory-dysarthric variant

Dorsomedial

38. Left Dorsomedial Pons: One-and-a-half syndrome

48. Left Dorsolateral Pons: Lateral pontine vestibulo-cerebellar–Horner syndrome
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate

Medulla
Ventromedial
49. Right Ventromedial Medulla: Classic medial medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops left weakness, impaired position sense, and difficulty moving the tongue.
50. Left Ventromedial Medulla: Classic medial medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops right weakness, impaired position sense, and difficulty moving the tongue.
51. Right Ventromedial Medulla: Medial medullary pure motor variant
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops acute left pure motor hemiparesis without cortical signs.
52. Left Ventromedial Medulla: Medial medullary pure motor variant
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops acute right pure motor hemiparesis without cortical signs.
53. Right Ventromedial Medulla: Motor–proprioceptive medial medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops left weakness and loss of limb position sense without vertigo or hoarseness.
54. Left Ventromedial Medulla: Motor–proprioceptive medial medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

Ventrolateral
55. Right Ventrolateral Medulla: Restricted spinothalamic medullary syndrome
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced
A patient develops isolated left body pain-temperature loss without weakness, facial numbness, vertigo, or dysphagia.
56. Left Ventrolateral Medulla: Restricted spinothalamic medullary syndrome
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

57. Right Ventrolateral Medulla: Spinothalamic–sympathetic syndrome without bulbar signs
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced
A patient develops left body pain-temperature loss and right Horner syndrome but no dysphagia or ataxia.
58. Left Ventrolateral Medulla: Spinothalamic–sympathetic syndrome without bulbar signs
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced
A patient develops right body pain-temperature loss and left Horner syndrome but no dysphagia or ataxia.
59. Right Ventrolateral Medulla: Caudal crossed spinothalamic–ipsilateral dorsal-column variant
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

60. Left Ventrolateral Medulla: Caudal crossed spinothalamic–ipsilateral dorsal-column variant
Evidence: Rare  |  Difficulty: Advanced

Dorsomedial
61. Right Dorsomedial Medulla: Dorsal-column nucleus syndrome
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops right loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia but no weakness.
62. Left Dorsomedial Medulla: Dorsal-column nucleus syndrome
Evidence: Moderate  |  Difficulty: Intermediate
A patient develops left loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia but no weakness.
63. Right Dorsomedial Medulla: Isolated central vestibular dorsal medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

64. Left Dorsomedial Medulla: Isolated central vestibular dorsal medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops abrupt persistent vertigo and severe imbalance without weakness, hearing loss, or bulbar symptoms.
65. Right Dorsomedial Medulla: Hypoglossal–dorsal column nucleus variant
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced

66. Left Dorsomedial Medulla: Hypoglossal–dorsal column nucleus variant
Evidence: Experimental  |  Difficulty: Advanced

Dorsolateral
67. Right Dorsolateral Medulla: Classic lateral medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, right facial numbness, and left body pain-temperature loss.
68. Left Dorsolateral Medulla: Classic lateral medullary syndrome
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

69. Right Dorsolateral Medulla: Nucleus ambiguus–predominant lateral medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

70. Left Dorsolateral Medulla: Nucleus ambiguus–predominant lateral medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops abrupt dysphagia, hoarseness, hiccups, and imbalance with little sensory complaint.
71. Right Dorsolateral Medulla: Sensory-predominant lateral medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core

72. Left Dorsolateral Medulla: Sensory-predominant lateral medullary variant
Evidence: Strong  |  Difficulty: Core
A patient develops left facial pain-temperature loss and right body pain-temperature loss with mild vertigo but no dysphagia.
Validation priorities
Run a 72 × 24 uniqueness audit: every case must have exactly one winning cell under its full finding set.
Review all Experimental templates first. The lateral midbrain and selected dorsal/ventrolateral medullary templates are most vulnerable to false precision.
For each case, verify that every positive and negative finding is anatomically compatible at the same axial level; do not mix rostral and caudal structures in one lesion.
Confirm side conventions for trochlear nuclear/fascicular lesions before using any CN IV case.
Use real-world variability in the debrief, even when the game uses binary hard exclusions.
After expert review, duplicate strong patterns with altered clue order rather than inventing unsupported new anatomy. This can expand replayability without reducing accuracy.
